All tests pass with no regressions.

Root cause: `getLegendItems()` in `AbstractCategoryItemRenderer` had an inverted null check — `if (dataset != null) { return result; }` — which caused it to return an empty legend whenever a dataset actually existed (and would have thrown an NPE via `dataset.getRowCount()` if it didn't). I corrected it to `if (dataset == null) { return result; }`, matching the intended early-return-on-no-dataset behavior. Compilation and the full test suite pass.

Test passes and no other tests broke.

The root cause was that `StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment` inserted the raw tooltip text into the HTML `title` attribute without escaping special characters, even though the class comment claimed this was fixed. The sibling generators (`OverLIBToolTipTagFragmentGenerator`, `DynamicDriveToolTipTagFragmentGenerator`) already used the existing `ImageMapUtilities.htmlEscape()` utility for this purpose. I updated `StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator` to call `ImageMapUtilities.htmlEscape(toolTipText)` as well, which correctly escapes quotes (and other HTML-significant characters) in the generated tag. Verified with `defects4j compile` and `defects4j test` — the target test now passes and no other developer tests broke.

Fixed. The root cause was a copy-paste bug in `ShapeUtilities.equal(GeneralPath, GeneralPath)`: `iterator2` was built from `p1.getPathIterator(null)` instead of `p2.getPathIterator(null)`, so the method always compared path 1 against itself and never detected differences with path 2. Corrected it to use `p2`, and all relevant tests now pass.

All tests pass with no regressions.

**Root cause:** `MultiplePiePlot(CategoryDataset dataset)` set `this.dataset = dataset` directly in the constructor instead of going through `setDataset(dataset)`, so the plot never registered itself as a `DatasetChangeListener` on the dataset passed in.

**Fix:** Removed the direct field assignment and called `setDataset(dataset)` at the end of the constructor (after the pie chart/paint setup it depends on), which registers the change listener and sets the dataset group as expected.

All tests pass with no regressions.

**Root cause:** In `BorderArrangement.arrangeFF`, when the left block's arranged width exceeds the container's fixed width constraint, `constraint.getWidth() - w[2]` becomes negative. This negative value was used to build a `Range(0.0, negative)` for constraining the right block, and also directly as the center block's fixed width, both of which are invalid (a `Range` requires lower ≤ upper). This mirrors a bug previously fixed in `arrangeFN` for the same reason (see the class's changelog comment).

**Fix:** Clamped both the right block's width range and the center block's width to be non-negative via `Math.max(..., 0.0)`, consistent with the existing pattern already used in `arrangeFN`.

All tests pass with no regressions.

**Root cause:** `removeDomainMarker`/`removeRangeMarker` in both `CategoryPlot` and `XYPlot` looked up the `ArrayList` of markers for a given renderer index from the foreground/background marker maps, but never checked whether that lookup returned `null` (which happens when no markers were ever added for that index/layer combination). Calling `.remove(marker)` on the `null` result threw an NPE.

**Fix:** In all four methods (`CategoryPlot.removeDomainMarker`, `CategoryPlot.removeRangeMarker`, `XYPlot.removeDomainMarker`, `XYPlot.removeRangeMarker`), added a `null` check on the retrieved `markers` list that returns `false` (marker not found/removed) instead of dereferencing a null list.

All tests pass, including the previously failing one.

**Root cause:** `PiePlot3D.draw()` called `initialise()` before checking whether the dataset was null/empty. `initialise()` unconditionally calls `DatasetUtilities.calculatePieDatasetTotal(dataset)`, which throws `IllegalArgumentException` for a null dataset. The existing null-dataset guard in `PiePlot3D.draw()` was located much later in the method, after `initialise()` had already been invoked, so it never had a chance to run (unlike `PiePlot.draw()`, which correctly checks for null/empty dataset before calling `drawPie()`/`initialise()`).

**Fix:** In `source/org/jfree/chart/plot/PiePlot3D.java`, moved the null/empty dataset check (draw "no data" message, restore clip, draw outline, return) to before the `initialise()` call, and removed the now-redundant duplicate check further down in the method.

All tests pass with no regressions.

**Root cause:** In `DefaultIntervalCategoryDataset`'s main constructor, when the dataset was constructed with zero series (e.g. `new double[0][0]`), `seriesKeys` and `categoryKeys` were explicitly set to `null` instead of empty arrays. Every method that iterates or indexes these arrays (`getSeriesIndex`, `getCategoryIndex`, `getRowCount`, `getColumnCount`, `clone`, etc.) assumed they were non-null arrays, causing `NullPointerException`s for empty datasets. Additionally, `setCategoryKeys` validated the new keys' length against `this.startData[0].length`, which throws for an empty `startData` array instead of correctly reporting zero categories.

**Fix:** Initialize `seriesKeys`/`categoryKeys` to empty arrays (`new Comparable[0]`) rather than `null` when there are no series, and changed `setCategoryKeys` to validate against `getCategoryCount()` (which already handles the empty case) instead of directly indexing `startData[0]`.

All tests pass, no regressions.

**Root cause:** `TimeSeries.clone()` unconditionally called `createCopy(0, getItemCount() - 1)`. For an empty series, `getItemCount()` is 0, so this became `createCopy(0, -1)`, which violates `createCopy`'s precondition `end >= start` and threw `IllegalArgumentException`.

**Fix:** In `clone()` (`source/org/jfree/data/time/TimeSeries.java`), only delegate to `createCopy` when the series has at least one item; for an empty series, build the clone via `super.clone()` with a fresh empty data list instead.

All four originally failing tests now pass, and the full developer test suite (`defects4j test`) reports 0 failures.

**Root cause:** In `DefaultKeyedValues.removeValue(int)`, the key→index map (`indexMap`) was only rebuilt when the removed item wasn't the last one in the list, leaving a stale mapping for the removed key when it *was* the last item — so `getIndex()` would return the old index instead of `-1` after removal, corrupting subsequent `setValue`/`addValue` calls (out-of-bounds `ArrayList.set`). Additionally, `removeValue(Comparable)` silently ignored unknown keys instead of throwing `UnknownKeyException` as documented and expected by callers/tests, and `DefaultKeyedValues2D.removeColumn(Comparable)` relied on that silent behavior, so making `removeValue` throw correctly required `removeColumn` to only remove the column from rows that actually contain it and to throw when the column key itself doesn't exist in the table.

**Changes** (all in `source/org/jfree/data/`):
- `DefaultKeyedValues.removeValue(int)`: always rebuild the index map after removal.
- `DefaultKeyedValues.removeValue(Comparable)`: throw `UnknownKeyException` for unrecognized keys instead of returning silently.
- `DefaultKeyedValues2D.removeColumn(Comparable)`: validate the column key exists (throwing `UnknownKeyException` otherwise), and only call `removeValue` on rows that actually contain that column key (since datasets can be sparse).

The root cause: `CategoryPlot.getDomainAxisIndex(CategoryAxis)` and `getRangeAxisIndex(ValueAxis)` didn't validate their argument, so calling them with `null` silently returned `-1` (via `List.indexOf(null)`) instead of throwing `IllegalArgumentException` as the tests expected; additionally, `getDomainAxisIndex` was missing the parent-plot lookup fallback that `getRangeAxisIndex` (and the analogous `XYPlot` methods) already had. I added a null check that throws `IllegalArgumentException` to both methods, and added the parent-plot fallback to `getDomainAxisIndex` for consistency with `getRangeAxisIndex`.

All tests pass with no regressions.

**Root cause:** In `DatasetUtilities.iterateDomainBounds` and `iterateRangeBounds` for `IntervalXYDataset`, when both interval bounds (e.g. `xLow`/`xHigh` or `yLow`/`yHigh`) were `NaN` for every item, or when only one bound was defined, the min/max accumulators were never updated. This meant `minimum` stayed `+Infinity` and `maximum` stayed `-Infinity`, causing the methods to return `null` (or an incomplete range), which then triggered a `NullPointerException` when the tests called `r.getLowerBound()`.

**Fix:** In both methods (source/org/jfree/data/general/DatasetUtilities.java), when one of the interval bounds is `NaN`, fall back to the other bound's value; when both are `NaN`, fall back to the dataset's actual x/y value for that item. This ensures a sensible range is still computed instead of silently producing an empty/null range.

All tests pass, no regressions.

Root cause: `ValueMarker`'s 6-argument constructor called `super(paint, stroke, paint, stroke, alpha)`, ignoring the `outlinePaint`/`outlineStroke` parameters entirely and using `paint`/`stroke` for both fill and outline. Fixed by passing `outlinePaint` and `outlineStroke` through to the `Marker` superclass constructor as intended. `source/org/jfree/chart/plot/ValueMarker.java:95`.

All tests pass with no regressions.

**Root cause:** In `DefaultBoxAndWhiskerCategoryDataset.add()`, when an item was added that overwrote the cell currently holding the cached range minimum or maximum, `updateBounds()` was called to invalidate the stale cache — but it simply reset `minimumRangeValue`/`maximumRangeValue` to `NaN` instead of recomputing them from the remaining data. The code right after then only compared the *newly added* item against these now-`NaN` values, so it completely lost track of the actual min/max coming from other cells in the dataset, producing an incorrect range.

**Fix:** Changed `updateBounds()` in `source/org/jfree/data/statistics/DefaultBoxAndWhiskerCategoryDataset.java` to properly rescan every item in the dataset and recompute `minimumRangeValue`/`maximumRangeValue` (and their row/column indices) from scratch, so the cache reflects the true bounds after an overwrite.

All tests pass, including the full developer test suite.

**Root cause:** `KeyedObjects2D` stores each row as a sparse `KeyedObjects` that only contains entries for column keys explicitly set on that row. Several methods incorrectly assumed every row contained every global column key:

- `getObject(Comparable, Comparable)` called `KeyedObjects.getObject(columnKey)` directly, which throws `UnknownKeyException` for a key not present in that particular row, instead of returning `null`.
- `removeColumn(Comparable)` called `KeyedObjects.removeValue(columnKey)` on every row unconditionally, throwing for rows that never had that column key.
- `removeRow(Comparable)` didn't validate the key, so an unrecognised key caused `removeRow(-1)` to throw an `IndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of `UnknownKeyException`.
- `removeObject(Comparable, Comparable)` had an empty/unimplemented "check whether the column is now empty" step, so columns were never pruned after their last value was nulled out.

**Fix:** In `source/org/jfree/data/KeyedObjects2D.java`, guard the row-level lookups with `KeyedObjects.getIndex(key) >= 0` checks before calling `getObject`/`removeValue`, added an `UnknownKeyException` check in `removeRow(Comparable)`, and implemented the column-emptiness check in `removeObject` so a column is removed once no row holds a non-null value for it.

**Root cause:** `MinMaxCategoryRenderer` had a Javadoc comment for an `equals()` override (added per the changelog) but the actual method body was never implemented, so it fell back to `Object.equals()` (reference equality), causing distinct instances with identical field values to compare unequal/inconsistently.

**Fix:** Implemented `equals(Object)` in `source/org/jfree/chart/renderer/category/MinMaxCategoryRenderer.java` to compare the `plotLines`, `groupPaint`, and `groupStroke` fields (using `PaintUtilities.equal` for the paint comparison), then delegate to `super.equals(obj)` for the inherited state, consistent with the class's own Javadoc and JFreeChart's usual equals pattern.

Root cause: `getPaint` clamped the input value into `v` but then used the unclamped `value` to compute the gray level `g`, so out-of-range values could produce a `g` outside 0–255 and throw `IllegalArgumentException` in `Color`. Fixed by using the clamped `v` in the calculation (`source/org/jfree/chart/renderer/GrayPaintScale.java:126`).

All tests pass, including the full developer suite.

**Root cause:** `StatisticalBarRenderer.drawHorizontalItem` and `drawVerticalItem` called `dataset.getMeanValue(row, column).doubleValue()` and `dataset.getStdDevValue(row, column).doubleValue()` unconditionally, throwing a `NullPointerException` whenever a dataset entry had a `null` mean or standard deviation (both are legitimately nullable in `StatisticalCategoryDataset`).

**Fix:** In `source/org/jfree/chart/renderer/category/StatisticalBarRenderer.java`, added a null check on the mean value that skips drawing the bar (returns early, since there's no bar to draw for a missing mean) and a null check on the standard deviation value that skips drawing the error indicator lines while still drawing the bar — applied symmetrically in both the horizontal and vertical drawing methods.

The root cause was in `Axis.drawLabel` (source/org/jfree/chart/axis/Axis.java): when an axis label's hotspot entity is added, the code called `plotState.getOwner()` and then immediately dereferenced the result (`owner.getEntityCollection()`) without checking whether it was `null`. When a chart is drawn with a `null` `ChartRenderingInfo` (as in `testDrawWithNullInfo`), the `PlotRenderingInfo` has no owning `ChartRenderingInfo`, so `getOwner()` returns `null`, causing an NPE during axis label rendering — this affected every category-plot-based chart, explaining the broad set of failing tests. The fix adds a `null` check around `owner` before using it, mirroring the existing `null` checks for `plotState` and `hotspot`. Verified with `defects4j compile` and `defects4j test` — all tests pass, no regressions.

All tests pass, including the previously failing `testCreateCopy3`.

**Root cause:** `TimeSeries.createCopy(int, int)` used `super.clone()` to build the copy, which copies the cached `minY`/`maxY` fields from the original series. Since `updateBoundsForAddedItem` (used when re-adding items to the copy) only *extends* the min/max range and never shrinks it, the copy retained stale bounds from data points that weren't actually included in the copied range (e.g., copying items 100.0/101.0 out of a series with max 102.0 still reported max 102.0). The changelog even noted an intended "clear minY/maxY cache in createCopy" fix that was never actually applied to the code.

**Fix:** Reset `copy.minY`/`copy.maxY` to `NaN` right after cloning in `createCopy(int, int)`, and in the empty-range branch of `createCopy(RegularTimePeriod, RegularTimePeriod)`, so the cached bounds are correctly recomputed from only the copied items.

All tests pass, no regressions.

**Root cause:** in `XYPlot.getDataRange(ValueAxis)`, the code that collects annotation bounds (`r.getAnnotations()`) was unconditionally dereferencing the renderer `r`, even though `r` can legitimately be `null` when a dataset has no renderer mapped to it (the surrounding domain/range-bounds code already null-checks `r`). This caused a `NullPointerException` whenever a plot's dataset had no associated renderer (e.g., scatter/step/area charts constructed via `ChartFactory` before a renderer is set).

**Fix:** wrapped the annotation-collection block in `source/org/jfree/chart/plot/XYPlot.java` with the same `if (r != null)` guard used elsewhere in the method, so it's simply skipped when there's no renderer for the dataset.

All tests pass with zero failures.

**Root cause:** In `XYSeries.addOrUpdate(Number, Number)`, when `allowDuplicateXValues` is `true` and the series is auto-sorted, the code assumed `indexOf(x)` always returned a negative "insertion point" encoding (as produced by `Collections.binarySearch` on a miss). But when a duplicate x-value already exists, `indexOf` returns a non-negative real index, and computing `-index - 1` from that produced an invalid (often negative) insertion index, causing the `IndexOutOfBoundsException`.

**Fix:** In `source/org/jfree/data/xy/XYSeries.java`, in the auto-sort branch of `addOrUpdate`, I now check whether `index` is negative (no match, safe to use the `-index-1` insertion-point formula) or non-negative (a duplicate x-value exists). In the latter case, I advance past any consecutive items sharing that x-value and insert the new item right after them, preserving both sort order and the order in which duplicate items were added — matching the expected test behavior (`getY(0)==1.0`, `getY(1)==2.0`).

All tests pass, no regressions.

**Root cause:** `ShapeList.equals()` delegated to `AbstractObjectList.equals()`, which compares stored elements with `ObjectUtilities.equal()`, i.e. plain `Object.equals()`. Several `Shape` implementations used in the list (e.g. `Line2D.Double`) don't override `equals()`, so two lines with identical coordinates were considered different, causing `equals()`/deserialization-equality checks to fail.

**Fix:** Overrode `ShapeList.equals()` (source/org/jfree/chart/util/ShapeList.java) to compare shapes element-by-element using `ShapeUtilities.equal()`, which correctly handles value-based equality for `Line2D`, `Rectangle2D`, `Ellipse2D`, `Arc2D`, `Polygon`, `GeneralPath`, etc., instead of relying on the generic `Object.equals()`-based comparison in the superclass.

All tests pass, no failures.

**Root cause:** In `TimePeriodValues.updateBounds()`, the block that updates `maxMiddleIndex` mistakenly referenced `this.minMiddleIndex` instead of `this.maxMiddleIndex` when computing the current max-middle value, so it compared against the wrong data item and left `maxMiddleIndex` stuck instead of updating it correctly. Fixed by changing the two `getDataItem(this.minMiddleIndex)` calls in that block to `getDataItem(this.maxMiddleIndex)`.

**Root cause:** The deprecated constructor `Week(Date time, TimeZone zone)` ignored the `zone` argument entirely, always delegating to `RegularTimePeriod.DEFAULT_TIME_ZONE` instead of the caller-supplied time zone. This caused the week number to be computed using the wrong time zone when a non-default zone was passed in.

**Fix:** Changed the delegation in `Week(Date, TimeZone)` (source/org/jfree/data/time/Week.java) to pass `zone` through instead of `RegularTimePeriod.DEFAULT_TIME_ZONE`, matching its documented behavior.

Root cause: in `TimeSeries.createCopy(RegularTimePeriod, RegularTimePeriod)`, when neither `start` nor `end` matches an actual data item and both fall between two adjacent existing items with `end` before the closest existing item to `start`, the computed `startIndex` ends up greater than `endIndex`. The code only checked for an empty range when `endIndex < 0`, missing the case where `startIndex > endIndex`, so it called `createCopy(start, end)` with a reversed range and triggered the `IllegalArgumentException`. Fix: also treat the range as empty when `endIndex < startIndex` (source/org/jfree/data/time/TimeSeries.java:944-946).

Root cause: `CommandLine.hasOption(String)` checked the `options` map directly by the given key, but `addOption` stores options keyed by the short option name and only records long-name→short-name mappings in the separate `names` map (used by `getOptionValues`). So `hasOption("debug")` for an option defined with short `-d`/long `--debug` never resolved the long name to its key and always returned false. Fixed by making `hasOption(String)` strip leading hyphens and resolve through `names` the same way `getOptionValues` already does.

**Root cause:** `Parser.setOptions()` assigned `this.requiredOptions` directly to the live list returned by `Options.getRequiredOptions()`, rather than a copy. Since `Options` instances are meant to be reusable across multiple `parse()` calls, and `Parser.processOption()` removes matched required options from that list as parsing proceeds, the shared `Options` object's internal `requiredOpts` list was being permanently mutated. After a first successful parse consumed a required option, a second parse with the same `Options` instance (but missing that option) would find an empty required-options list and incorrectly succeed instead of throwing `MissingOptionException`.

**Fix:** In `src/java/org/apache/commons/cli/Parser.java`, changed `setOptions()` to copy the required options into a new `ArrayList` each time parsing starts, so mutations during one parse no longer leak into the shared `Options` object for subsequent parses.

The root cause was in `HelpFormatter.appendOption`: when building the usage line, it appended `" <" + argName + ">"` whenever `option.hasArg() && option.getArgName() != null`, without checking whether the arg name was empty. Since `Option.getArgName()` can be set to `""`, this produced `-f <>` instead of omitting the placeholder. The `renderOptions` method already had a correct helper for this (`option.hasArgName()`, which checks for non-null and non-empty), so I made `appendOption` use the same `hasArgName()` check for consistency, which resolves the defect without special-casing the test's specific value.

**Root cause:** `GnuParser.flatten()` only special-cased the `-Dproperty=value` pattern (splitting off the first two characters as the option). For inputs like `-f=bar`, `-foo=bar`, or `--foo=bar` it never recognized the `=` separator, so it either passed through the raw `=value` (including the `=`) as the option's argument, or failed to recognize the option at all for the double-dash long form.

**Fix:** In `src/java/org/apache/commons/cli/GnuParser.java`, before falling back to the `-D`-style special case, check whether the substring before the first `=` matches a known option (short or long, with `-`/`--` prefix stripped). If so, split the token into the option and its value at the `=` sign, correctly handling `-f=bar`, `-foo=bar`, and `--foo=bar`.

**Root cause:** `GroupImpl.process()` re-invokes an anonymous `Argument`'s `process()` (and thus `ArgumentImpl.processValues()`) every time it encounters another unmatched token, since `ArgumentImpl.canProcess()` always returns `true`. Each invocation reset its local `argumentCount` to `0`, so the argument's declared `maximum` was enforced only *per call* instead of *cumulatively* across all the tokens it ever consumed. For a `SourceDestArgument` with a max of 2 fed 4 values, this let it silently swallow all 4 values instead of leaving the extra tokens unconsumed, so the parser produced an `ARGUMENT_UNEXPECTED_VALUE` error from deep inside `SourceDestArgument.validate()` (mentioning the wrong sub-argument, e.g. `"input"`) instead of the expected top-level `UNEXPECTED_TOKEN` error from `Parser.parse()`.

I found a leftover orphaned Javadoc block in `WriteableCommandLine.java` (a comment describing "values that don't include defaults" with no method attached), which was the tell that a method had been stripped out here. I restored a `getUndefaultedValues(Option)` accessor (interface + `WriteableCommandLineImpl` implementation) that returns only the values genuinely added via `addValue`, excluding any programmatic defaults, and used it in `ArgumentImpl.processValues()` to seed `argumentCount` with the number of values already consumed for that option. This correctly enforces the maximum cumulatively across repeated invocations while leaving option defaults (which never call `addValue`) unaffected.

Verified with `defects4j compile` and `defects4j test`: the target test now passes and the full developer suite reports 0 failing tests.

All tests pass, no regressions.

**Root cause:** `GroupImpl.validate` (src/java/org/apache/commons/cli2/option/GroupImpl.java) validated each required option twice: once unconditionally because `option.isRequired()` was true, and again because `commandLine.hasOption(option)` was true. For a present option, `FileValidator.validate` had already replaced the `String` values in the list with `File` instances on the first pass; the second pass then tried to cast those `File` objects back to `String`, throwing `ClassCastException`.

**Fix:** Changed the validation logic so a present option is validated exactly once (via the "present" branch), and the "required/Group" branch only fires when the option is *not* present — preserving the original behavior of detecting missing required options and recursively validating unfulfilled nested groups, while eliminating the double validation of present options.

All tests pass, including the two previously failing ones, with no regressions.

**Root cause:** `WriteableCommandLineImpl.getValues(Option, List)` returned either the user-supplied values *or* the registered default values, but never merged the two. When a user supplied fewer values than the argument's configured defaults (e.g., one value where two defaults were registered), the trailing default values were simply discarded instead of being used to fill the remaining slots.

**Fix:** In `getValues`, after determining the value list actually supplied by the user, I pad it out with any remaining registered default values (from index `valueList.size()` onward) when the supplied list is shorter than the option's default list — in `src/java/org/apache/commons/cli2/commandline/WriteableCommandLineImpl.java`.

All target tests pass and the full developer suite (0 failures) confirms nothing else broke.

**Root cause:** the `Option` interface had javadoc for `getParent()`/`setParent()` but the actual method declarations were missing, so no implementation ever tracked an option's containing `Group`. As a result, when a child option (e.g. inside a nested group, or a `Command`/`DefaultOption`) was added to the command line, its parent `Group` was never registered as present. This made `GroupImpl.validate()` unable to count the parent group towards its min/max restrictions (`BugCLI123Test` failures) and made `WriteableCommandLineImpl.getOptions()` omit ancestor groups from the ordered options list (`testGetOptions_Order` failures).

**Fix:**
- Restored `Option.getParent()`/`setParent(Option)` declarations (`Option.java`).
- Implemented them in `OptionImpl` with a simple `parent` field.
- `GroupImpl`'s constructor now calls `option.setParent(this)` for each option it contains.
- `WriteableCommandLineImpl.addOption` now walks up the newly available parent chain and adds any not-yet-present ancestor groups to the internal `options` list (without touching the trigger-name map, since a group's `getTriggers()` aggregates all its children's triggers and must not overwrite the direct trigger→option mappings).

Verified with `defects4j compile` and `defects4j test`: all previously failing tests now pass, and the full developer suite reports 0 failures.

All tests pass with no regressions.

**Root cause:** In `PosixParser.burstToken`, when bursting a clustered short-option token (e.g. `-azc`) and a non-option character was hit with `stopAtNonOption` set, the code called `process(...)` to stash the remainder as an argument but did not stop the bursting loop. The loop then kept scanning subsequent characters (`c` in this case), found it matched a valid option, and incorrectly added `-c` as a parsed option even though parsing should have stopped at the first non-option character.

**Fix:** Added a `break` after the `process(token.substring(i))` call in `burstToken` (src/java/org/apache/commons/cli/PosixParser.java) so that once a non-option character forces a stop, no further characters in the token are processed.

All tests pass, including the previously failing `testStop2`, with no regressions.

**Root cause:** In `PosixParser.processOptionToken`, when a two-character token like `-z` was not a recognized option and `stopAtNonOption` was true, the code set `eatTheRest = true` but never added the token itself to the output tokens list — it was silently dropped. The subsequent tokens were then gobbled verbatim and re-parsed downstream as if they were fresh options, causing `-a` to be wrongly recognized as set.

**Fix:** Changed `processOptionToken` to call the existing `process(token)` helper (already used for the equivalent case in `burstToken`) instead of just setting the flag. `process` correctly preserves the unmatched token (prefixed with the `--` marker) before the rest of the arguments are gobbled as literal args.

All tests pass with no failures.

**Root cause:** In `PosixParser.processOptionToken`, when a 2-character token like `-z` wasn't a recognized option and `stopAtNonOption` was `false`, the token was silently dropped instead of being added to the flattened token list. `Parser.parse` relies on scanning the flattened tokens to detect unrecognized options and throw `UnrecognizedOptionException`, so a dropped token meant the exception was never raised.

**Fix:** In `src/java/org/apache/commons/cli/PosixParser.java`, added an `else` branch to `processOptionToken` so unrecognized 2-character option tokens are still added to the token list (matching the existing behavior for unrecognized bursted tokens in `burstToken`), allowing `Parser.parse` to detect and report them correctly.

All 0 failures, and the diff is a minimal, targeted change confined to `src/java`.

**Root cause:** In `PosixParser.flatten()`, when a token longer than 2 characters starts with `-` and isn't itself a registered option (e.g. `-something` following `-t`), it was unconditionally handed to `burstToken()`, which splits it character-by-character looking for single-letter options. When none of the leading characters matched a known option, each was emitted as a bogus separate token (`-s`, `-o`, `-m`, ...), corrupting the argument stream and eventually causing `UnrecognizedOptionException: Unrecognized option: -o`. This ignored the fact that the immediately preceding option (`-t`) still needed an argument value.

**Fix:** In `src/java/org/apache/commons/cli/PosixParser.java`, before bursting such a token, check whether there's a pending option that requires an argument and whether the token's first character isn't itself a valid option letter. If so, the token is treated as the literal value for that pending option (via the existing `process()` helper) instead of being burst apart. If the first character *is* a valid option (e.g. `-bvalue`, `-pfile1:file2`), bursting proceeds as before, so existing combined-flag/burst behavior is preserved.

All tests pass with no regressions.

**Root cause:** `PosixParser.flatten` handled `--foo` / `--foo=bar` tokens by unconditionally splitting on `=` and adding the pieces, without ever checking whether the long option was actually recognized or honoring `stopAtNonOption`. As a result, an unrecognized long option like `--zop==1` was split and injected into the token stream, causing the downstream `Parser.parse` loop to treat `"--zop"` as the (invalid) option that triggers `eatTheRest`, but the value `=1` and subsequently-burst tokens from later short options had already been split apart — producing 7 stray argument tokens instead of leaving the original 3 raw args intact.

`FlowSensitiveInlineVariables.Candidate.canInline()` decides whether to inline a definition's right-hand side directly into a later use. **Root cause:** In `PeepholeSubstituteAlternateSyntax.tryMinimizeIf`, the optimization that merges `if (cond) lhs = a; else lhs = b;` into `lhs = cond ? a : b;` only checked that `lhs` itself had no side effects. It didn't account for the fact that this merge reorders evaluation: normally `cond` runs first and the assignment (including evaluation of any computed LHS, like `x[y]`, or the implicit read of the LHS for a compound assignment like `x += ...`) runs second, whereas the merged form evaluates the LHS before `cond`. When `cond` has a side effect that changes a value the LHS depends on (e.g. `x[--y]` where `y` is used as both the array index and mutated in the condition), the merge silently changes program semantics.

**Fix:** The merge is now only allowed unconditionally when it's a plain `ASSIGN` to a simple `NAME` (in which case only the RHS moves into the hook, preserving evaluation order relative to `cond`); for any other case (compound assignment ops, or a computed LHS such as `GETELEM`/`GETPROP`) the merge is skipped if `cond` may have side effects, falling back to the safe generic `cond ? then : else` statement-level transform instead.

## Root cause

`CrossModuleMethodMotion` moves prototype methods into later modules, but `AnalyzePrototypeProperties` (which decides what's safe to move) had two gaps for the `Foo.prototype = {method: function(){...}}` object-literal form of prototype declaration:

1. **Missing global-scope check.** The move requires the prototype's owner (`Foo`) to be a global name so the code generated in the later module (`Foo.prototype.method = JSCompiler_unstubMethod(...)`) can actually reference it. This condition was documented in a comment in `CrossModuleMethodMotion.moveMethods` (item #4) but never actually implemented — so a method whose class was really a local variable (e.g. `var jQuery2 = function(){}` declared inside an IIFE) still got moved, producing a dangling reference to `jQuery2` in a module where it isn't in scope.

2. **Missing scope context for closure-variable detection.** For the chained form (`Foo.prototype.bar = function(){...}`), each property gets its own `NameContext` on the analysis stack, so reads of outer-scope variables inside the method body are correctly attributed to that property (blocking motion). For the object-literal form (`Foo.prototype = {bar: function(){...}}`), no such context was ever pushed — the function value was treated as an anonymous, untracked node — so a method that read a genuine closure variable (like `theLoneliestNumber`) was never marked as closure-sensitive and was moved anyway, again producing broken code.

## Fix

In `AnalyzePrototypeProperties.java`:
- Added `getPrototypeLiteralPropertyName`, which recognizes when a `FUNCTION` is the value of a key in an object literal being assigned to some object's `.prototype`, and pushes a proper `NameContext` for that property name (instead of the generic anonymous context) so closure-variable reads are correctly attributed.
- Added `isGloballyReachable`, and in `processPrototypeParent` check whether the `.prototype` owner resolves to a non-global variable; if so, mark the property's `NameInfo` as closure-sensitive (reusing the existing "cannot be moved" mechanism), preventing the motion pass from moving it.

**Root cause:** `JSType.checkEquivalenceHelper` used a single boolean `tolerateUnknowns` flag to implement two semantically different notions of "equivalence tolerant of unknown types": (1) *invariance*, where the unknown type should be considered compatible with any type, and (2) *data-flow* comparison, where two types are considered the same only if *both* are unknown. Both `isInvariant()` and `differsFrom()` funneled into the same code path (`return thisUnknown && thatUnknown;`), so `isInvariant()` incorrectly required both sides to be unknown instead of treating unknown as compatible with everything. This made `RecordType.isSubtype`'s declared-property check (`propA.isInvariant(propB)`) reject records whose property types were structurally covariant only because one used `?` (unknown) as a return/param type — exactly the case in `testSubtypeWithUnknowns2` and in the `TypeCheckTest.testIssue791` regression (`function(): undefined` vs `function(): ?`).

**Fix:** introduced a 3-valued `EquivalenceMethod` enum (`IDENTITY`, `DATA_FLOW`, `INVARIANT`) and threaded it through `checkEquivalenceHelper` and its helpers in `JSType`, `UnionType`, `RecordType`, `ArrowType`, and `FunctionType` in place of the ambiguous boolean. `isEquivalentTo` now uses `IDENTITY`, `differsFrom` uses `DATA_FLOW` (unchanged behavior: same only if both unknown), and `isInvariant` uses the new `INVARIANT` semantics (unknown is invariant with everything), fixing the defect without altering any other equivalence behavior.

**Root cause:** `FlowSensitiveInlineVariables` gathers inlining candidates by looking up the reaching definition of a variable using the dataflow state *entering* the enclosing CFG node (`MustBeReachingVariableDef.getDef`, which reads `state.getIn()`). This is correct across CFG-node boundaries, but a single CFG node can itself contain internal control flow, e.g. a ternary (`HOOK`). In `var i = 0; return 1 ? (i = 5) : 0, i;`, the whole `return` statement is one CFG node, so the trailing use of `i` was resolved against the pre-statement definition (`var i = 0`), ignoring the conditional reassignment `i = 5` that executes earlier within that same statement. The pass then wrongly inlined `0` for the final `i` and stripped the initializer from `var i`.

## Root cause

The compiler has special-case handling in `TypedScopeCreator` for the common `Foo.prototype = {...}` idiom, based on the assumption that "prototype sets are always declared" (an explicit comment in the code). However, the code following that comment never actually enforced it — `isQualifiedNameInferred` always fell through to treating such assignments as *inferred*. Because of this:

- The `Foo.prototype` scope variable was unconditionally un-declared when an object literal was assigned to it, but never re-declared, since the "declared" code path that would redeclare it was unreachable. This left `scope.getVar("Foo.prototype")` `null`, causing the NPE in `testPropertiesOnInterface2`.
- Whether `Foo.prototype`'s new properties (e.g. `alert`, `bar`, `baz`) became visible to code that referenced `Foo.prototype` (or captured it in a variable) *before* the reassignment depended entirely on `TypeInference`'s flow-sensitive, single-pass analysis — which only sees the mutation *after* it occurs in the control-flow order, not before (`testMethodBeforeFunction2`'s `y`, and the IIFE-scoped case in `testIssue1023`).

In `src/com/google/javascript/jscomp/TypedScopeCreator.java`:
1. `isQualifiedNameInferred` now actually implements "prototype sets are always declared": a `Foo.prototype = {...object literal...}` assignment is treated as declared (when it's safe to do so — see below), so the qualified-name slot for `Foo.prototype` is properly re-declared instead of being silently dropped.
2. Since declaring `Foo.prototype` early (during `TypedScopeCreator`, before `TypeInference` runs) means the object literal's own property types must be known immediately, `processObjectLitProperties` gained a `useValueTypeFallback` option: when a key has no real declared type (no JSDoc), it falls back to the type already computed for its value node (e.g. a function literal), and declares it as an *inferred* property (not a declared one) to preserve prior semantics and avoid spurious duplicate-declaration warnings for repeated keys.

## Root cause

`TypedScopeCreator.isQualifiedNameInferred` had a blanket rule: any qualified name ending in `.prototype` is treated as an always-declared (non-inferred) property, based on the comment "Prototypes of constructors and interfaces are always declared." **Root cause:** `FunctionInjector.canInlineReferenceDirectly` (the gate that decides whether a call can be replaced in-place by substituting the function's return expression) only rejected an argument if it either had its own side effects or "might mutate state" *and* was referenced more than once. It missed two other unsafe/undesirable cases:

1. **Evaluation-order hazard**: if the argument's *value* could be changed by some other side effect that executes earlier in the returned expression (e.g. `function foo(a){return modifiyX() + a;} foo(x);`), direct substitution moves the argument's evaluation from "before the call" to "wherever `a` is textually used," which can happen *after* a side effect that would have altered `x`. This silently changed semantics.
2. **Uncontrolled duplication**: if the parameter was referenced more than once, the argument expression got duplicated verbatim, even when it wasn't a cheap/immutable value (e.g. a nested pure call like `f(1)`), causing needless code bloat instead of falling back to block-style inlining (or not inlining at all).
3. Additionally, "mutable-state" arguments (e.g. `[]`, `new Date`) were only blocked when referenced *more than once*, but should be blocked whenever referenced *at all* in direct-substitution mode, matching the policy already used for block inlining.

**Fix (all within `src/com/google/javascript/jscomp/FunctionInjector.java`):**
- Changed the mutable-state guard to trigger on any reference (`> 0` instead of `> 1`).
- Added a check (`isParameterReferencedAfterSideEffect`, backed by a small `ParameterReferenceCheck` visitor and `hasShallowSideEffect` helper) that rejects direct inlining when an argument that `canBeSideEffected` is referenced after another side-effecting sub-expression in the returned expression.
- Added a `canDuplicateWithoutBloat` check that rejects direct inlining when a parameter is referenced more than once and the argument isn't cheap to duplicate (mirrors the existing "large" check used for block inlining).

## Root cause

`ClosureCodingConvention.getSingletonGetterClassName()` recognizes the `goog.addSingletonGetter(Ctor)` idiom only when the constructor argument is a qualified name (`callArg.getNext().getQualifiedName()`). `NameAnalyzer`'s dead-code-elimination pass (`smartNamePass`) relies on this to mark such calls as "only affects class definition," so the whole call/definition can be dropped if the class is otherwise unused.

The defect had two related root causes in the unique-name-generation machinery used by function inlining:

1. **`NodeTraversal.traverse(Node root)`** didn't special-case a `FUNCTION` node passed as the traversal root. It pushed a scope for the root, then called `traverseBranch`, which for a `FUNCTION` node dispatches to `traverseFunction`, which pushes the *same* function's scope a second time. `FunctionToBlockMutator` traverses a cloned function body this way (`NodeTraversal.traverse(compiler, fnNode, ...)`), so `MakeDeclaredNamesUnique`'s `InlineRenamer` ended up declaring the function's parameters/locals twice, wasting unique-id numbers and causing generated names like `b$$inline_3` instead of the expected `b$$inline_1`. Fixed by making `traverse(Node root)` enter the function's scope once and traverse its name/params/body directly, mirroring the existing pattern already used by `traverseAtScope`.

2. Separately, in **`MakeDeclaredNamesUnique`**, a named function expression's own name (its "recursive name") was being resolved using the function's *inner* (parameter/body) scope instead of its own outer "recursive name" scope, because `NodeTraversal.traverseFunction` visits a function-expression's name node after the inner scope has been pushed. This let a same-named local `var` inside the body incorrectly rename the function's own declaration name too. Fixed by renaming the function-expression name immediately when it's registered (using the correct scope) and marking that node so the later generic `NAME` visit doesn't re-resolve it against the wrong scope.

**Root cause:** When JSDoc type parsing failed with a syntax error (e.g. `@type function */`, where `function` is not followed by `(`), the code path that detected the error consumed the terminating token (which was often the comment-closing `*/`, i.e. `EOC`) via `next()`/as a method parameter, but never gave that token back to the token stream. The outer annotation-processing loop in `JsDocInfoParser.parse()` also skipped calling `eatTokensUntilEOL()` entirely when the recorded type was `null`, relying instead on a stale local `token` variable. As a result, the parser lost track of having already reached the `*/` marker and went on to request another token from an already-exhausted stream, producing a spurious "Unexpected end of file" warning in addition to the expected type-syntax warning.

**Fix (in `src/com/google/javascript/jscomp/parsing/JsDocInfoParser.java`):**
1. In the `@type`/`@typedef`/`@this`/etc. annotation handling, moved the `token = eatTokensUntilEOL();` call so it always runs after a type expression is parsed, whether or not that parse succeeded, keeping the loop's recovery logic consistent regardless of failure.
2. In `parseFunctionType`, `parseBasicTypeExpression`, and `parseTypeName`, called `restoreLookAhead(token)` before reporting a type-syntax error, so the token that triggered the error (often `EOC`/`EOF`) is pushed back onto the stream instead of being silently discarded. This lets the recovery logic correctly detect end-of-comment/end-of-file instead of over-reading past it.

**Root cause:** In `CheckAccessControls.checkPropertyVisibility`, two bugs prevented correct detection of illegal overrides of `@private` properties:

## Root cause

`DeadAssignmentsElimination.isVariableStillLiveWithinExpression` decides whether a dead-looking assignment inside a compound expression (`||`, `&&`, `?:`) might still be read later along some execution path. The buggy version treated `OR`/`AND`/`HOOK` parents exactly like any other node — it just scanned the *following siblings* in document order and stopped at the first READ/KILL — ignoring that:
- for `OR`/`AND`, the right operand may not even execute (short-circuiting), so a KILL found there must not be treated as a guaranteed kill;
- for `HOOK`, only one of the two branches executes, so both branches must be checked and a KILL only counts if *both* branches kill (mirroring the existing `checkHookBranchReadBeforeKill` helper), which the fallthrough switch never invoked correctly.

Additionally, `isVariableReadBeforeKill`'s `OR`/`AND` case unconditionally skipped checking the first operand (treating it like a `HOOK`'s non-executed condition), even though the first operand of `||`/`&&` always executes. This caused a definite kill in the first operand (e.g. `a = 3` in `(a=3)||a`) to be missed, so a preceding dead assignment (`a = 2` in `(a=2)||(a=3)||a`) was incorrectly kept alive.

## Fix

In `src/com/google/javascript/jscomp/DeadAssignmentsElimination.java`:
- `isVariableStillLiveWithinExpression`: added proper `OR`/`AND` handling (only trust a READ from the right operand, since it may not execute) and proper `HOOK` handling (use `checkHookBranchReadBeforeKill` only when at the condition position, and otherwise skip the sibling branch entirely).
- `isVariableReadBeforeKill`: for `OR`/`AND`, check the first (always-executed) operand first and return its result if conclusive; only fall back to the (conditionally executed) second operand for a possible READ.

## Root cause

`JSType.isEmptyType()` only ever considers a type "empty" if it *is* a `NoType`/`NoObjectType`/`NoResolvedType`. However, the type system also defines `LEAST_FUNCTION_TYPE` (`(All...) -> NoType`) as the bottom of the function-type lattice (see `FunctionType.supAndInfHelper`, which returns `LEAST_FUNCTION_TYPE` as the infimum of two unrelated function types). Since `FunctionType` never overrode `isEmptyType()`, this bottom type was never recognized as empty.

This mattered in `JSTypeRegistry.canPropertyBeDefined`, which uses `!alt.getGreatestSubtype(type).isEmptyType()` to decide whether a property could plausibly be defined on a type. When checking `s.toLowerCase.indexOf(...)` in `testIssue301`, the infimum of the unrelated function types `Array` (which had `indexOf` assigned to it) and `String.prototype.toLowerCase` correctly evaluated to `LEAST_FUNCTION_TYPE`, but because that wasn't recognized as empty, the checker wrongly concluded `indexOf` *could* be defined on `toLowerCase`, suppressing the expected "Property indexOf never defined" warning.

## Fix

Made `isEmptyType()` non-final in `JSType` and overrode it in `FunctionType` to also treat an ordinary function whose return type is empty (i.e. `LEAST_FUNCTION_TYPE`) as empty, while preserving the base behavior via `super.isEmptyType()` (needed because `NoObjectType`/`NoType` themselves extend `FunctionType`).

## Root cause and fix

`UnreachableCodeElimination.tryRemoveUnconditionalBranching` tries to remove a useless `break`/`continue`/bare `return` when its CFG target equals the node that control would fall into if it were removed. To handle chains of useless jumps (`break -> break -> break`), it recursed into whatever jump statement it found as the fall-through target and removed that one too, all within a single visit.

This over-cascading caused two bugs:

1. **`testCascadedRemovalOfUnlessUnconditonalJumps`**: since `CompilerTestCase` runs each pass twice (`getNumRepetitions() == 2`), removing an entire chain of jumps in one traversal caused two applications to wipe out the whole chain, whereas the expected behavior is to unwind exactly one link of the chain per application.
2. **`testIssue311`**: cascading into a jump statement that lives elsewhere in the tree (reachable only by following fall-through past an `if`/`else`) removed a node before `NodeTraversal` — which caches a node's "next sibling" *before* recursing into it — got a chance to visit it. `NodeTraversal` then tried to visit that already-detached node again, and `removeDeadExprStatementSafely` crashed with an NPE trying to remove a node whose parent was already `null`.

Fix: only the node that was originally passed to `visit()` (the "top-level" node) is actually removed; if resolving its fall-through leads to another jump statement, that statement is left untouched (it gets handled on its own turn, or on the next repetition of the pass). I also added a defensive check in `removeDeadExprStatementSafely` to no-op on an already-detached node, guarding against the general hazard of `NodeTraversal`'s cached "next" pointers becoming stale. With these changes, `defects4j test` reports 0 failing tests across the whole suite.

This is unsound in general — a constructor can alias its result (e.g. by capturing `this` in a closure), so `new X()` results should only be considered local when the caller-supplied `locals` predicate says so (matching how `GETPROP`/`GETELEM`/other cases already defer to `locals.apply(value)`), just as the existing TODO comment noted. **Fix:** in `src/com/google/javascript/jscomp/NodeUtil.java`, the `Token.NEW` case in `evaluatesToLocalValue` now returns `locals.apply(value)` instead of unconditionally `true`.

## Root cause

Per ES3 semantics (and an existing but unimplemented TODO comment in `FunctionType.resolveInternal`), when a function is called with `null`/`undefined` as its receiver, the runtime coerces `this` to the global object rather than leaving it null. So a JSDoc `@this` type that includes `null`/`undefined` in a union (e.g. via a backwards-referenced `@typedef {(Array|null|undefined)}`) should be treated, for type-checking purposes, as if the nullable/undefined parts were stripped out.

Two places didn't implement this:

1. `FunctionType.resolveInternal` resolved the `@this` type but only accepted it if it was directly an `ObjectType`; a nullable union type (not itself an `ObjectType`) was silently discarded, leaving `typeOfThis` as the unresolved `NamedType` placeholder — which is why the error messages showed the raw typedef name (`goog.MyTypedef`) instead of the resolved type.
2. `FunctionTypeBuilder.ThisTypeValidator` rejected any `@this` type that wasn't a subtype of `Object`, without first stripping null/undefined, so a legitimately nullable-but-otherwise-object `@this` type triggered a spurious `THIS_TYPE_NON_OBJECT` warning.

## Fix

- In `FunctionType.resolveInternal`, call `restrictByNotNullOrUndefined()` on the resolved `@this` type before checking `instanceof ObjectType`, so nullable object unions properly become the concrete object type used for `this` inside the function body.
- In `FunctionTypeBuilder.ThisTypeValidator`, apply the same `restrictByNotNullOrUndefined()` before checking subtype-of-`Object`, so a nullable `@this` type doesn't spuriously warn as long as its non-null/undefined part is an object.

## Root cause

`TreeList.AVLNode.removeSelf()` handles removing a node with two children by copying the in-order successor's *value* into the current node object and detaching the successor node from the tree — but it never mutates the successor's own `left`/`right`/`relativePosition` fields, since it's simply discarded. `TreeListIterator.remove()` used to cache a reference to that soon-to-be-discarded node in its `next` field (`next = next.next()`) before calling `parent.remove()`, relying on that node's stale internal links for the next `previous()`/`next()` call. Since the node was removed from the tree without its fields being reset, calling `.previous()` on it returned incorrect data — reproduced by the failing test, which expected `"A"` but got `"C"`.

In `TreeListIterator.remove()` (`TreeList.java`), stop caching the successor node across the removal — reset `next = null` unconditionally after `parent.remove(currentIndex)`, so the next `next()`/`previous()` call recomputes the node fresh via `nextIndex` (an existing code path already present for this purpose). Also simplified the index bookkeeping to a single `parent.remove(currentIndex)` call with `nextIndex--` only when `currentIndex < nextIndex`, equivalent to the two previous branches but without the stale-reference bug.

`TarArchiveInputStream.read()` treated end-of-underlying-stream the same whether or not the current tar entry's declared size had actually been reached: if the wrapped `InputStream` returned `-1` (e.g. because the archive was truncated mid-entry), the code just set `hasHitEOF = true` and returned `-1`, silently truncating the entry's data instead of signaling an error. **Root cause:** `BitInputStream.readBits` caches bits in a single 64-bit `long` (`bitsCached`/`bitsCachedSize`). The fill loop kept reading whole bytes as long as `bitsCachedSize < count` (count up to 63). When `bitsCachedSize` was already in the high 50s, adding one more full byte (8 bits) could push the logical size past 64, silently shifting real data bits out of the 64-bit register (an actual bit overflow), corrupting both the current read and all subsequent reads.

**Fix (`src/main/java/org/apache/commons/compress/utils/BitInputStream.java`):** Capped the fast-path fill loop at `bitsCachedSize < 57` so it never overflows the register. If more bits are still needed after that, only the exact number of bits required from the next byte are merged into the cache to complete the read (respecting little/big-endian bit ordering), and the leftover bits of that byte are preserved and reinstated as the new cache contents right after extraction — so no data is ever lost, just deferred correctly to the next call.

## Root cause

In `CSVFormat.printAndQuote()` (MINIMAL quote mode), the code unconditionally quoted a value whenever it was the first field of a record and its first character wasn't alphanumeric:

```java
if (newRecord && (c < '0' || c > '9' && c < 'A' || c > 'Z' && c < 'a' || c > 'z')) {
    quote = true;
}
```

This treated any leading symbol — including a plain backslash, which has no special meaning unless an escape character is configured — as requiring quoting, even though RFC4180's TEXTDATA range already permits such characters unquoted. It incorrectly forced quoting for values like `\` or `\\`.

This makes quoting decisions based on actual characters that require it rather than an unrelated "is it alphanumeric" rule.

## Root cause

Both `UTF8StreamJsonParser` and `ReaderBasedJsonParser` had incomplete implementations of the JACKSON-105 fix ("eager number parsing misses errors"): the number-parsing methods (`_parseNumber`, `_parserNumber2`/`_parseNumber2`, `_parseFloat`) all contained a comment `// As per #105, need separating space between root values; check here`, and there was even a leftover Javadoc block for a `_verifyRootSpace` method — but the method body itself, and the calls to it, were missing. ## Root cause

`StdDateFormat._format()` was supposed to output ISO-8601 years beyond the normal `[1,9999]` range (per Jackson issue #2167: extended years, and BCE dates), but the implementation was incomplete/buggy:

1. `pad4()` was written assuming years never exceed 4 digits: it split the value as `h = value/100` and ran that quotient through `pad2()` (which only handles 0–99). For a 5-digit year like `10204`, `h=102` overflowed `pad2`'s digit computation and printed a stray `:` character (`Character` arithmetic wrap: `'0'+10` = `:`), producing `":204"` instead of `"10204"`.
2. There was no era handling at all — BCE dates were formatted using `Calendar.YEAR` directly (always positive under `GregorianCalendar`), so year 0 (BCE 1) printed as `"0001"` instead of the required `"+0000"`, and there was no code path emitting `+`/`-` signs at all (a leftover comment block described the intended BCE handling but no code implemented it).

## Fix

## Root cause

In `DeserializationContext.handleUnknownTypeId`, if a `DeserializationProblemHandler` resolves an unknown type id to `Void.class`, that's treated as a special sentinel and the method returns `null` to its caller (meaning "map this to null, not an error"). In `TypeDeserializerBase._findDeserializer`, when this happens and no default-impl deserializer exists either, the code called `_handleUnknownTypeId` again, got `null` back for the same reason, and then — despite a comment saying it should *not* do this — literally returned `null` as the "deserializer" to use. Callers (e.g. `AsArrayTypeDeserializer._deserialize`) then invoked `deser.deserialize(...)` on that `null` reference, causing the `NullPointerException` reported by the test.

## Fix

In `src/main/java/com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/jsontype/impl/TypeDeserializerBase.java`, when the handler signals "no type" via the `Void.class` sentinel, return `NullifyingDeserializer.instance` (already used elsewhere in the same class for the analogous default-impl case) instead of `null`, so callers get a real, safe deserializer that simply produces `null` values. **Root cause:** `MappingIterator.nextValue()` had no real recovery logic — after a deserialization failure (e.g. `UnrecognizedPropertyException`) partway through a value, it only called `_parser.clearCurrentToken()`. This left the underlying parser positioned mid-object/array, so the next `nextValue()` call resumed parsing from wherever the failed value left off (e.g. a nested field's value), producing garbage results or spurious follow-on errors instead of correctly locating the next sibling value.

This lets iteration continue cleanly with the next sibling value, matching the intended "read recovery" behavior described in the (previously unimplemented) comments in the class.

## Root cause

When a `@JsonCreator` constructor takes a single `Collection`-typed parameter (e.g. `List<MessageWrapper>` or `List<String>`), `CreatorCollector.addDelegatingCreator` classifies it as an **array delegate** creator (`_arrayDelegateDeserializer`) rather than a plain delegate (`_delegateDeserializer`), since the parameter is collection-like.

**Root cause:** `QueryParser` special-cased the top-level `,` character (comma group-selectors, e.g. `"a, b"`) with a hand-rolled loop that used `tq.chompTo(",")` to grab each subsequent alternative. `chompTo` does a plain literal-character scan, so it split apart sub-queries containing an unrelated comma inside brackets/parens (e.g. `li:matches([0-9,]+)`), corrupting the extracted regex and causing `Pattern.compile` to throw (`handlesCommasInSelector`). ## Root cause

`Tokeniser.consumeCharacterReference` parses named character references using `CharacterReader.consumeLetterSequence()`, which only consumes ASCII letters. HTML entity names like `sup1`, `sup2`, `sup3`, `frac14`, `frac12`, `frac34` end in digits, so the reader stopped at `sup`/`frac`, matched that shorter (also valid) entity name, and left the trailing digits as literal text — producing `⊃1;` instead of `¹`.

## Fix

Added `CharacterReader.consumeLetterThenDigitSequence()` (`src/main/java/org/jsoup/parser/CharacterReader.java`), which consumes a run of letters followed by a run of digits, and switched `Tokeniser.consumeCharacterReference` (`src/main/java/org/jsoup/parser/Tokeniser.java`) to use it instead of `consumeLetterSequence()`. This lets the tokeniser capture the full entity name (including trailing digits) before falling back character-by-character to find the longest matching known entity.

The analogous non-escaped state (`ScriptDataEndTagName`) didn't have this bug, confirming it was a spurious extra advance. I removed the erroneous `r.advance();` line.

## Summary

**Root cause:** In JDK versions used here, `Charset.isSupported(name)` / `Charset.forName(name)` throw `IllegalCharsetNameException` (unchecked) for syntactically invalid charset names, instead of just returning `false`. `DataUtil.getCharsetFromContentType` and `DataUtil.parseByteData` assumed these calls could only ever return `false` for bad names, so malformed/empty/duplicated `charset=` values from HTTP headers or HTML5 `<meta charset>` tags crashed the parser instead of gracefully falling back to the default charset. Additionally, the charset-extraction regex didn't stop at commas or single quotes, so multi-value or single-quoted charset declarations captured garbage (e.g. `"ISO-8859-1,"`), and a duplicated `charset=charset=X` value wasn't unwrapped.

**Fix (`src/main/java/org/jsoup/helper/DataUtil.java`):**
- Tightened `charsetPattern` to also stop at commas and single quotes, so quoted (`'UTF-8'`) and multi-charset (`charset=X, charset=Y`) content types are parsed correctly.
- In `getCharsetFromContentType`, strip a repeated leading `charset=` prefix, treat an empty extracted value as "not found", and catch `IllegalCharsetNameException` around the `Charset.isSupported` checks, returning `null` (the documented fallback) instead of propagating the exception.
- In `parseByteData`, wrapped the meta-charset re-decode step in a try/catch for `IllegalCharsetNameException`, falling back to the default charset when the HTML declares a broken charset (e.g. an unterminated attribute like `<meta charset=UTF-8">`).

**Root cause:** jsoup's tokeniser tracked whether a self-closing `/` flag on a start tag had been "acknowledged" by the tree builder, but never distinguished *why* it went unacknowledged. For known non-void tags (e.g. `<div/>`, `<font/>`) the tree builder deliberately left the flag unacknowledged, and the tokeniser's generic top-of-`read()` check fired a vague, misleading error ("Self closing flag not acknowledged") on the next token read — instead of a proper diagnostic. Additionally, that generic check itself raced ahead of the actual tag being dispatched whenever character data (e.g. an entity reference) was buffered immediately before the self-closing tag, since `read()` can return the buffered characters while leaving the tag token still pending; the flag was already flipped false by the underlying scan, causing the generic check to fire prematurely on a token it hadn't even returned yet.

1. `HtmlTreeBuilder.insertEmpty` now explicitly reports `"Tag cannot be self closing; not a void tag"` when a known, non-void tag carries the self-closing flag, and always acknowledges the flag once handled (both for void and non-void known tags).
2. `Tokeniser.read()` only performs its generic "flag not acknowledged" check when it's about to start scanning fresh input (`!isEmitPending`), so it no longer misfires on a tag token that's merely queued behind buffered characters from the same underlying scan.

**Root cause:** jsoup's HTML tree builder had no support for the HTML5 `<template>` element's special parsing rules. When a `<template>` appeared as a child of `<thead>`/`<tbody>`/`<tr>` (any "in table"-family insertion mode), it was treated like an arbitrary foreign element: `InTable`'s fallback (`anythingElse`) enabled foster-parenting and reprocessed it via `InBody`, moving the `<template>` element (and thus losing its intended children) out of the table entirely instead of keeping its content nested inside it.

**Fix (`src/main/java/org/jsoup/parser/HtmlTreeBuilder.java` and `HtmlTreeBuilderState.java`):** Implemented the HTML5 spec's template-handling rules:
- Added a template insertion-mode stack (`pushTemplateMode`/`popTemplateMode`/`currentTemplateMode`) to `HtmlTreeBuilder`, and made `resetInsertionMode` aware of `template` on the stack.
- Made `clearStackToTableContext`/`...TableBodyContext`/`...TableRowContext` stop at a `template` boundary (matching spec), so descending into a template inside a table doesn't corrupt the open-elements stack.
- Added explicit `template` start/end tag handling in `InHead` (insert normally, no fostering, switch to a new `InTemplate` state; on close, pop stack/formatting markers and reset insertion mode).
- Added a new `InTemplate` state that dispatches table-related tags to their proper insertion modes (or `InBody` for everything else), per spec.
- Routed `template` tags through `InHead`/`InTemplate` instead of the generic fallback in `InTable` and `InBody` (added to `Constants.InBodyStartToHead` and end-tag handling), so `<template>` is never subject to foster parenting.

**Root cause:** In `NumberUtils.createNumber`, the hex-literal branch decided whether to return an `Integer`, `Long`, or `BigInteger` purely by counting characters after the `0x`/`#` prefix. **Root cause:** In `TypeUtils.getTypeArguments(Class<?>, Class<?>, Map)`, the hierarchy-walking loop stopped early whenever it encountered *any* class with its own declared type parameters (`cls.getTypeParameters().length > 0`), regardless of whether that class was the original subject being queried or was reached mid-climb from a subtype. 2. Conversely, it accidentally masked a real raw-type-erasure scenario (a subclass extending a generic ancestor without supplying type witnesses, e.g. `EClass<T> extends DClass`) as if it were a normal case, which happened to produce a passing (but accidental) result for one assertion while failing others.

- Stop only once the target class is actually reached (`toClass.equals(cls)`).
- Separately, stop accumulating further type-variable mappings only when a generic class with its own type parameters is reached *via recursion* (`subtypeVarAssigns != null`), since that specifically indicates the class was referenced by an ancestor in raw/unparameterized form (an erasure event), so its parameters genuinely can't be resolved further. The root cause was incomplete/incorrect handling of Unicode supplementary characters (surrogate pairs) in `StringUtils`'s character-search methods: `indexOfAny(CharSequence, char[])`, `containsAny(CharSequence, char[])`, `indexOfAnyBut(CharSequence, char[])`, `containsNone(CharSequence, char[])`, and `indexOfAnyBut(String, String)`. Each of these matched individual `char` values without verifying that a matched high surrogate was actually paired with the correct low surrogate (or, conversely, incorrectly treated a lone/unpaired high surrogate as a full BMP match). This caused false positives/negatives whenever inputs contained supplementary characters (code points above U+FFFF, like `U+20000`) or broken/lone surrogate halves.

I fixed each method to properly check `Character.isHighSurrogate(ch)` and, when true, compare the following surrogate in both the search set and the sequence before treating it as a match — falling back to a plain match only when a full pair can't be checked (e.g., end of string, matching the built-in `String.indexOf` semantics for broken pairs). This brought all five methods in line with the behavior already correctly implemented elsewhere in the class (e.g. `contains(CharSequence, CharSequence)`).

**Fix:** In `StringUtils.java`, when a matching character is a high surrogate, the method now also checks the following low surrogate (in both `cs` and `searchChars`) before declaring a match, falling back to a true match only if no low surrogate is available (mirroring `String.indexOf` semantics). Non-surrogate characters are matched as before.

**Root cause:** In the continued-fraction constructors of `Fraction` and `BigFraction`, when converting a double to a fraction with a `maxDenominator` limit (epsilon fixed at 0), the loop computes the next convergent `p2/q2` and checks for `long` overflow *before* checking whether `q2` already exceeds `maxDenominator`. **Root cause:** `CMAESOptimizer`'s bounded-search transform normalized variables linearly (`(x - lower) / (upper - lower)` and its inverse). When one bound has a vastly larger magnitude than the other (e.g. lower=-20, upper=5e16), this arithmetic silently absorbs/cancels the meaningful digits of `x` at double-precision granularity — e.g. `decode` could only resolve values in steps of 8.0 instead of fractions of a unit — so the optimizer could get stuck far from the true optimum whenever it was near the boundary of a very wide range.

**Fix** (`src/main/java/org/apache/commons/math3/optimization/direct/CMAESOptimizer.java`):
- Replaced the linear `encode`/`decode` with a numerically robust transform: it computes the fractional position always relative to whichever bound has the smaller magnitude (avoiding combining a modest value with an astronomically larger one), and maps that fraction through an `asin`/`sin` half-angle transform onto an unconstrained internal coordinate. This keeps `decode` always feasible and preserves precision near either boundary regardless of how large the opposite bound is.
- Since the transform now always produces feasible points, removed the now-unnecessary repair/penalty/feasibility-retry machinery (`repair`, `penalty`, `isFeasible`, `isRepairMode`, `setValueRange`), simplifying `FitnessFunction.value()` to just decode-and-evaluate.
- Updated the initial-sigma computation to derive the internal step size from the actual local derivative of the new transform at the start point (via `encode(start + step) - encode(start)`), instead of a simple division by the (possibly huge) range, since the linear approximation no longer applies uniformly.

**Root cause:** In `RectangularCholeskyDecomposition`, the pivoted-Cholesky algorithm had two related bugs:

1. When searching for the diagonal element with maximal value to pivot to the current position `r`, the code compared candidates against `index[swap[i]]` instead of the running-best `index[swap[r]]`. Since `swap[i]` for `i > r` held stale values from earlier rounds (or default `0`), pivot selection was essentially random for matrices with more than 3 rows.
2. Once a pivot swap between position `r` and a later position was decided, the code swapped the `index` permutation array but never moved the already-computed partial rows of the `b` (root) matrix for columns `0..r-1`. Since those partial factor values are tied to the *position*, not the row label, failing to swap them along with `index` left the root matrix associated with the wrong rows, producing a matrix whose product `B·Bᵀ` was a partially-permuted (and thus incorrect) version of the original matrix.

**Fix:** corrected the running-max comparison to use `index[swap[r]]`, and added a loop to swap the corresponding `b[r][0..r-1]` and `b[swap[r]][0..r-1]` entries whenever `index[r]` and `index[swap[r]]` are swapped.

**Root cause:** `PearsonsCorrelation.getCorrelationPValues()` computed the two-sided p-value as `2 * (1 - tDistribution.cumulativeProbability(t))`. Internally, `TDistributionImpl.cumulativeProbability(t)` for `t > 0` returns `1.0 - 0.5 * beta`, where `beta` is the regularized incomplete beta value. This removed the now-unused `TDistribution`/`TDistributionImpl` imports. Since `SpearmansCorrelation` delegates its p-values to `PearsonsCorrelation`, this single fix resolves both failing tests.

## Root cause

In `SingularValueDecompositionImpl`, `getU()` (case `m >= n`) and `getV()` (case `m < n`) build the missing side of the decomposition via a recurrence `W = B·E·S⁻¹`, where `E` is the eigenvector matrix of the tridiagonal `Bᵗ·B` (or `B·Bᵗ`). I introduced a field `maxP = min(max, numberOfEigenvalues)` — the number of eigenvectors actually requested from the eigen-decomposition *before* the trailing non-positive ones are discarded — and used `maxP` (instead of `p`) as the row bound when extracting the eigenvector submatrix and running the `W` recurrence in both `getU()` and `getV()`. This supplies the recurrence with full-length eigenvectors whenever eigenvalues were dropped due to natural rank deficiency, while leaving behavior unchanged when the caller explicitly truncates below `maxP` via the `max` constructor argument (the pre-existing, still-passing `testTruncated` case).

## Root cause

`LocalDate.fromCalendarFields`/`LocalDateTime.fromCalendarFields` used `calendar.get(Calendar.YEAR)` directly as the ISO proleptic year, but `Calendar.YEAR` is the *year-of-era* — always positive — and ignores `Calendar.ERA`. `fromDateFields(Date)` had the same bug in a sneakier form: it used the deprecated `Date.getYear()+1900`. I verified experimentally that `Date.getYear()` returns the *identical* value for AD year N and BC year N (e.g. both AD 1 and BC 1 give `getYear() == -1899`), because the deprecated Date accessors don't retain era information at all — so no arithmetic on `date.getYear()` can ever recover the era. The only reliable fix is to reconstruct a `Calendar` from the `Date`'s millis (which *does* recover era correctly) and reuse the corrected `fromCalendarFields` logic.

In `src/main/java/org/joda/time/LocalDate.java` and `LocalDateTime.java`:
- `fromCalendarFields`: convert year-of-era to proleptic year by checking `calendar.get(Calendar.ERA) == GregorianCalendar.BC`.

## Root cause

`DateTimeZone.adjustOffset(instant, earlierOrLater)` is used to pick the earlier/later valid offset at a DST overlap. The buggy code:

1. Compared *local* millis 3 hours before/after the instant (`instantBefore == instantAfter`) to detect "no overlap" — but two local instants 6 hours apart are essentially never equal, so this guard never worked as intended and it never distinguished a gap from an overlap.
2. Passed those local millis values into `convertLocalToUTC(..., originalInstantUTC)` as if they were UTC instants, even though `convertLocalToUTC` expects an actual UTC instant for that parameter (it calls `getOffset` on it). Feeding it a local instant made it pick the wrong offset entirely, which is why `withLaterOffsetAtOverlap()` returned `-02:00` instead of `-03:00`.

## Fix

Rewrote `adjustOffset` in `src/main/java/org/joda/time/DateTimeZone.java` to:
- Compute the actual offsets 3 hours before/after (`offsetBefore`, `offsetAfter`) instead of local timestamps, and bail out early when `offsetBefore <= offsetAfter` (no overlap — equal is normal, offset increasing is a gap, not handled here).
- Compute the local instant and derive the two UTC candidates (`local - offsetBefore`, `local - offsetAfter`), verifying each is self-consistent via `getOffset` before treating the local time as genuinely duplicated.
- Return the appropriate candidate directly based on `earlierOrLater`, instead of delegating to `convertLocalToUTC` with a mismatched parameter type.

**Root cause:** `BaseChronology.get(ReadablePeriod, long duration)` — used by `Period(long)`/`Duration.toPeriod()` to split a bare millisecond duration into fields — trusted `DurationField.isPrecise()` unconditionally. For fields like `days`/`weeks`, `ZonedChronology`'s duration fields report `isPrecise() == true` whenever the chronology's zone has a fixed offset (no DST), since a calendar day genuinely is exactly 24h there. That's correct for real interval-based calculations, but a bare `long duration` has no associated instant/zone context, so exploiting that "precise because fixed offset" property caused `Period(length)`/`Duration.toPeriod()` to leak the JVM's default zone into the result — populating `weeks`/`days` (e.g. `weeks=64`) instead of leaving them at 0 and rolling everything into `hours`, whenever the default zone happened to be a non-UTC fixed offset.

**Fix:** In `BaseChronology.get(ReadablePeriod, long duration)` (src/main/java/org/joda/time/chrono/BaseChronology.java), only trust a field's zone-dependent precision when the chronology's zone is `null`/UTC (the one case where there's no ambiguity about a reference instant). For any other zone, only fields that are inherently precise regardless of zone (sub-12-hour units: hours, minutes, seconds, millis) are used; larger units always fall through unused, exactly as the standard/no-zone case already worked.

**Root cause:** In `DateTimeParserBucket.computeMillis`, saved fields are applied once, in an order that (correctly) puts `year`/`weekyear` before `monthOfYear` before `weekOfWeekyear`. For patterns mixing a calendar year/weekyear with `monthOfYear` and `weekOfWeekyear` (e.g. `"yyyy-MM-ww"` or `"xxxx-MM-ww"`), setting the year/weekyear first followed by month leaves the working date in a weekyear that differs from the target one (e.g. Jan 1, 2010 actually falls in ISO weekyear 2009). Applying `weekOfWeekyear` afterward then adjusts the week *within that stale weekyear*, producing a date roughly a year off (e.g. `2008-12-29` instead of `2010-01-04`).

**Fix:** After the normal single pass of setting the saved fields, when `resetFields` is requested, re-apply all saved fields a second time using the already-adjusted `millis` as the new base (`src/main/java/org/joda/time/format/DateTimeParserBucket.java:350-358`). This second pass lets the year/weekyear field re-anchor the date that was already corrected by the week field on the first pass, converging on the intended date for the ambiguous field combinations while remaining a minimal, general change (no special-casing of specific field values).

**Root cause:** `DateTimeZone.getOffsetFromLocal(long)` estimates the offset for a local time by computing an initial guess, adjusting, and recomputing. When the two estimates agreed, the method assumed the local time was unambiguous and returned that offset directly. However, for zones with a positive UTC offset (e.g. Moscow, +04:00 → +03:00), during a DST "fall back" overlap both the initial and adjusted estimates can land on the *later* (post-transition, smaller-offset) reading of the ambiguous window, since the naive estimate happens to be internally consistent there. This caused ambiguous local times to always resolve to the later/standard offset instead of the earlier/daylight offset mandated by the documented "always favour daylight time" contract — the opposite asymmetry from the already-handled DST gap case.

**Fix:** In `src/main/java/org/joda/time/DateTimeZone.java`, when the two offset estimates agree, I added a check against the previous zone transition: if reinterpreting the local time using the offset that was in effect just before that transition would still map to a UTC instant prior to the transition (i.e. the old offset is also a valid interpretation), then we're in the second reading of an overlap, so the earlier (larger, pre-transition) offset is returned instead. This generalizes correctly regardless of the sign of the offset, since it's derived algebraically rather than special-cased for Moscow.

**Root cause:** `ZonedChronology.ZonedDateTimeField.set(long instant, int value)` converted the instant to local time, applied the field change, then converted back to UTC via `DateTimeZone.convertLocalToUTC(localInstant, false)`, which has no way to know which of two valid offsets to prefer when the resulting local time falls in a DST overlap (e.g., setting `secondOfMinute`/`minuteOfHour`/`hourOfDay` near a "fall back" transition). **Root cause:** `ZonedChronology.ZonedDurationField.add()` (used by field-based durations like `years()`, `months()`, `weeks()`, `days()`) converted a local instant back to UTC using `DateTimeZone.getOffsetFromLocal()` directly. During a DST overlap (e.g. the repeated 02:30 wall-clock time on 2011-10-30 in Europe/Berlin), a local time is ambiguous — `getOffsetFromLocal` always resolves it to the *earlier* (summer/+02:00) offset, discarding which of the two actual instants the calculation started from. So adding zero years/months/weeks/days to a "second occurrence" (+01:00, winter) instant silently shifted it to the "first occurrence" (+02:00, summer) instant.

The sibling class `ZonedDateTimeField.add()` (used for `year()`, `monthOfYear()`, etc.) already avoided this by calling `DateTimeZone.convertLocalToUTC(localInstant, false, instant)`, which prefers the *original* instant's offset when the local time is ambiguous.

## Summary

**Root cause:** `GJChronology` combines the Julian calendar (no year zero) before the cutover with the proleptic Gregorian calendar (has year zero) after it. Two related defects caused this to break down:

1. `GJChronology.getInstance(...)` never validated that the cutover instant falls after year zero. The rest of the class (comments in `ImpreciseCutoverField.add` even say so explicitly) assumes this invariant, so a cutover at or before year 0 silently produced an inconsistent chronology instead of being rejected.
2. When `ImpreciseCutoverField.add()` (used for `year`/`weekyear` arithmetic) computed a new value using the Gregorian field's own zero-inclusive arithmetic and that value crossed into the Julian (pre-cutover) side, the resulting year/weekyear label was reinterpreted verbatim as a Julian value. Since the Julian calendar has no year zero, this either threw `IllegalFieldValueException` (when the raw result was exactly 0) or was off by one (since Gregorian year -1 and Julian year -1 don't represent the same point in time — the Julian calendar's missing year 0 needs to be "skipped").

**Fix:**
- In `assemble()`, reject a cutover whose Gregorian year is `<= 0`, matching the invariant the rest of the class already relies on.
- In `ImpreciseCutoverField.add(int/long)`, when the Gregorian-computed year (or weekyear) lands at or below zero after crossing the cutover gap, subtract one extra year before converting to the Julian side, compensating for the year that Julian skips. (The reverse direction, Julian→Gregorian, already works correctly since Julian's own field is skip-zero-aware internally, and direct `set()`-based construction, used e.g. by `BuddhistChronology`, is intentionally left untouched since it already performs its own zero-adjustment via `SkipUndoDateTimeField`.)
